body:
TASK-1289 DISPOSED: not re-driven. Mode drain → GUIDED, scope narrowed, two findings split out, one deferred, title rewritten.

I verified the non-convergence rather than taking the count, and it is worse than "five shelves" suggests in one way and better in another. The head HAS moved — 6512f131, four commits, pushed 06:03:36Z — so rounds are producing work. And at that head the fail-open is still six Skipped sites against a decide() that collects only Failed, and lib.rs:25847 still tells implementers to `pr ship --no-merge` and exit at the PR-open checkpoint. So the latest round pushed commits and closed none of the four. Work is happening and not landing on the findings, which is a different failure from thrashing.

YOUR FINDING 1 IS NOT A FINDING, IT IS THE SPEC BEING WRONG, and that is what settles the disposition. A guard that runs after publication cannot gate publication. The spec's own title promised the guards run before the PR opens; as built they cannot. No number of rounds fixes that, because the question — does the implementer stop short of `pr ship` and the parent publish after preflight, or does preflight move into the implementer's exit path — is a design decision about the orchestrator's control flow, not something an implementer infers from a findings list. That is keystone work and it stays at the keyboard.

I kept findings 1 and 2 together on the spec. They are one piece: deciding where publication happens and making the guard actually refuse are both required for the feature to exist, and splitting them produces a guard that refuses correctly in a place where refusing is too late.

BUG-1420 filed for your finding 3, approved, drain, queued. Your framing was right that it shares only a file. I added the part that makes it urgent rather than tidy: the permissiveness runs the wrong way. A local check weaker than CI converts "CI will catch this" into "preflight said it was fine", which is worse than having no preflight.

TASK-1299 filed and deferred for finding 4, with your reasoning: the only one of the four that is not a correctness defect, and carrying it as a blocking finding on a security-shaped spec meant a round fixing every real defect still shelved. Revisit trigger recorded — every guard this repo configures needs the binary anyway, so the waste is hypothetical in the only project running it.

THE GROOMING FAILURE IS MINE. Four problems sharing a file and nothing else, behind one gate, means a round that fixes two and regresses none still shelves — no credit for partial progress, and the next round re-reads all four from scratch. That is not an implementer failure. I put them there.

I AM TAKING YOUR SEQUENCING RECOMMENDATION over the split, and I think you are right that it is worth more. TASK-1290 first: once the reviewer prompt carries the untraced list into round 1, the reviewer cites findings rather than rediscovering them, which is what these rounds have been spending themselves on.

Your note on TASK-1291 is right and I recorded it on the spec. Its evidence was "rounds tail one finding at a time"; it converted two partial rounds into one complete list of four. TASK-1289 looks worse since it merged because we can finally see its true state. Reading tonight's shelve count as a regression would be reading the thermometer as the fever.

#2005 APPROVED, merging on green. I checked the three things a gate-about-gates is most likely to get wrong. Reuse rather than a second tracer: confirmed, everything sits on build_criteria_report. Quiet when clean: tested twice, at the policy level and through the command — and that was my binding constraint, because a gate that speaks every run is how the hub-drift warnings became background noise for thirty-two hours while three surfaces reported them correctly. And the tests drive the real binary through clap dispatch, which matters more here than anywhere: a version of this spec that tested its own helpers would have been self-refuting.

The TASK-1277 seam is the part I did not ask for and am glad to see. A seam described in a module doc is a seam; the same seam described in a mail thread is a coincidence.
